$comment: Accepted risks for the container security review (scripts/auditContainerImage.mjs).
Same philosophy as scripts/secure-egress-allowlist.json: an entry does not hide a
finding, it explains one. An accepted risk still appears in the report, marked
ACCEPTED RISK and printed with its reason and its compensating control, so a reviewer
reads the decision rather than a silence.
Every entry must state a reason and a compensatingControl. An entry MAY narrow itself
with a covers[] list naming the exact paths it excuses; anything the list does not name
stays an open finding. Keep covers[] as narrow as the evidence — that is what makes a
NEW world-writable path or a NEW setuid binary visible even though its neighbours are
expected. Never accept a check wholesale to quiet it.
Deliberately NOT accepted, though both are known and intentional:
/var/www/html being world-writable and non-sticky (FS-01). The reason is sound — the
entrypoint must delete and recreate root-owned files as an arbitrary UID, which an
overlay filesystem only permits in a writable, non-sticky directory — and APP-02
states that mechanism in full. But a world-writable directory holding the PHP that
Apache executes is exactly the decision a reviewer must make for themselves, so the
report puts it in front of them as an open finding with the rationale attached rather
than resolving it on their behalf.
The compiler and package managers inherited from the base image (CFG-04). Real
remediation exists (a slimmer final stage, or a read-only root filesystem), so it
stays open as an improvement rather than being written off.
The root default (CFG-01). --user 33:33 works today with no change to the image,
and a hardened deployment should set it. The image keeps the root default only
because the entrypoint's port-80 back-compat listener is root-only, and removing
it would silently break a deployment still mapping to the container's port 80.
Closing this is a release decision about a documented compatibility guarantee,
not a fix, so the finding stays open with its one-flag remedy attached.

FS-01.reason: These are the base image's own scratch directories and the application's three data directories. Apache needs its lock, socket and log paths writable before it drops privilege; the application needs the cache, upload and wind directories writable under whatever UID the runtime assigns, which is not known at build time.
FS-01.compensatingControl: Run with a read-only root filesystem and mount each of these as tmpfs or as a volume, so what is writable is decided by the deployment rather than by the image, and nothing written survives a restart.

PRV-01.reason: The base images are selected by tag on purpose, so that a rebuild picks up the distribution's current security patches without anyone having to act. Pinning them by digest would freeze the base: advisories would then accumulate between deliberate bumps, and IMG-03 — the count a rebuild can close, 13 of 1547 today — would climb steadily instead of staying near zero. The trade is build reproducibility against patch currency, and for a project that rebuilds on every release, patch currency is worth more.
PRV-01.compensatingControl: Reproducibility is enforced one level up, where it decides what actually runs: the deployment pins the APPLICATION image by digest rather than by tag, and the hardened-install guide's verification step compares the digest a task is running against the digest recorded at push time. So the bytes in production are pinned and checked even though the base image floats. The residual risk — that two builds of the same source can differ in their base layers — is accepted, and this report records the base image's advisory load on every run, so a base that drifts somewhere harmful is visible rather than silent.

FS-03.reason: The Debian base image's account and mount utilities. None is invoked by Sitrec, by Apache or by the entrypoint; they are present because the base image ships a general-purpose userland.
FS-03.compensatingControl: Start the container with no-new-privileges (--security-opt no-new-privileges, or allowPrivilegeEscalation: false). The setuid bit is then inert whatever is on disk, so the binaries cannot raise privilege even if a process reaches them.
